name: Gunung Padang
hook: A claimed Ice Age pyramid inside a Javan megalith hill; the paper was retracted in 2024.
claim: By 2013 Natawidjaja's team (TTRM) claimed man-made layers 14,000+ years old lie deep inside Gunung Padang hill. Their 2023 paper: a natural lava hill 'sculpted' and encased 25,000–14,000 BCE, then buried and built phases to 5500 BCE, 20–30 m deep, with chambers.

claimed_age.label: Oldest phase 25,000–14,000 BCE (~27,000–16,000 cal BP)
claimed_age.basis: OxCal-calibrated 14C on 12 bulk organic-soil samples (6 cores, 6 trenches): 8 AMS at Beta Analytic, 4 conventional at BATAN. Also claimed: Unit 3 buried 7900–6100 BCE; Unit 2 built 6000–5500 BCE.

accepted_age.label: Terraces ~117–45 BCE (charcoal); deep layers not shown built
accepted_age.basis: Press report: Yondri (BRIN, outside the team) had charcoal from under terrace walls 14C-dated at BATAN: Terrace 1 ~117 BCE, Terrace 4 ~45 BCE; calibration unreported. S1 put the terraces at 2000–1100 BCE.

orthodoxy_at_claim.label: A megalithic terrace complex sitting on the hilltop, used for ancestor worship; the rock layers below were read as natural.

key_proponents: Tim Terpadu Riset Mandiri (TTRM) Gunung Padang
key_critics: Anonymous experts in geophysics, archaeology and 14C

unambiguous_signal.note: The deep evidence was geophysical layers, cores and soil dates, not artifacts. In July 2013 IAAI archaeologists called the results hypothesis without strong archaeological evidence.

documented_context.note: Cores and trenches were logged against geophysics, but whether the layers were built or natural was the open question; the team says Layer 2 was once read as natural rock.

multiple_dating_methods.note: All ages were radiocarbon (on bulk soil in S1); no second dating method was applied to the deep layers.

multiple_labs.note: 12 bulk-soil samples: 8 AMS at Beta Analytic, 4 conventional at BATAN (S1, 2023). Both labs dated bulk soil, so the second lab does not address the association problem.

professional_recovery.note: Geologists and geophysicists cored and trenched the site; archaeologist Ali Akbar led the TTRM archaeology team (Oct 2011–2014).

peer_reviewed_report.note: Through 2018 the claim appeared in a popular book (Akbar 2013, S10) and a preprint (2018). The first peer-reviewed report came in 2023 and was retracted in 2024.

material_accessible.note: Outside archaeologists worked on the surface terraces (Yondri), but no outside team re-examined the deep layers. Supporting data were posted publicly only in 2024 (S11).

independent_teams.note: All deep geophysics, coring and dating came from the Natawidjaja-led team. In 2024 Ali Akbar said no other team had dug the disputed 6–11 m.

proponent_stake.note: Team formed under a presidential special staffer; Natawidjaja wrote a book linking the site to Plato's Atlantis (S9). S8 analyses the nationalist framing of the 'pyramid'.

objections.text: The radiocarbon dates came from soil samples not associated with any artifact or feature that could reliably be interpreted as man-made.
objections.outcome_note: Upheld by the journal's investigation. The authors dispute it, saying the soils come from man-made rock layers with small artifacts, shown only in their correspondence (S12).

objections.text: The 'pyramid' is a natural volcano, older than human occupation, with an archaeological site on its surface; the buried layers are more likely natural.
objections.raised_by: Anonymous third-party experts (Dec 2023); critics in Nature news (S4)
objections.outcome_note: S1 itself calls the core (Unit 4) a natural lava hill. That Units 2–3 are natural is argued but not yet shown by a published geological study.

objections.text: The 14C dates may not even date the soils accurately, since soils are notoriously difficult to date.
objections.raised_by: Anonymous third-party experts (critique sent to authors 19 Dec 2023)
objections.outcome_note: Not tested independently; all 12 dates in S1 were on bulk organic soil.

objections.text: GPR, ERT and seismic tomography can map subsurface layers but cannot identify a cultural layer; the team's work is geology, not archaeology.
objections.outcome_note: Consistent with the retraction's finding that no man-made feature was tied to the dated soils (S2).

objections.text: The team's results were still hypothesis, without sufficiently strong archaeological evidence.
objections.raised_by: Truman Simanjuntak & Daud Tanudirjo (IAAI discussion, July 2013)
objections.outcome_note: No archaeological evidence for the deep phases has been published since; the 2023 paper was retracted on this point (S2).

objections.text: There is no evidence people had the skills to build a pyramid as early as 25,000–14,000 BCE.
objections.outcome_note: No evidence of such building skills at that date has been published since.

status_note: Refuted as published: the only peer-reviewed evidence was retracted in 2024 because the dated soils had no shown link to human work. The authors reject this, citing unpublished artifacts; no outside team has dug the disputed 6–11 m.
what_settled_it: Third-party experts in geophysics, archaeology and radiocarbon raised concerns. The journal's co-editors and Wiley found a major error: the dated soils were not associated with any artifact or feature reliably interpreted as man-made, so the paper was retracted in 2024.

timeline.event: N.J. Krom records the site and describes it as a place of ancestor worship.
Three local farmers rediscover the site; government archaeological studies follow.
Yayasan Turangga Seta claims pyramids under several West Java mountains, including Gunung Padang, citing ancestral guidance.
The team later called TTRM begins work at the site (Oct 2011–2014), eventually digging to 4–11 m.
Ali Akbar's book dates the team's Layer 3 (5–30 m deep) to about 14,000 years.
At a July IAAI discussion, archaeologists call the team's results hypothesis without strong archaeological evidence.
Team posts a preprint claiming a layered, pyramid-like structure predating 10,000 BP.
Archaeological Prospection publishes the paper (20 Oct): oldest phase 25,000–14,000 BCE.
The co-editors and Wiley retract the paper: dated soils not tied to man-made features. All authors disagree.
Authors publish a response rejecting the retraction, citing small artifacts shown only in correspondence with the journal.
Co-editor Eileen Ernenwein publishes a reflection: the false claim got through because of peer-review oversights.

decisive_tests.test: Publish depth and context records for the 12 dated samples, and have outside archaeologists examine the small artifacts the authors say accompany Units 1–3.
decisive_tests.would_show: Whether any cultural material is securely associated with the dated soils.

decisive_tests.test: Independent controlled excavation across the Unit 1–3 boundary to 6–11 m, AMS-dating short-lived material (charcoal, seeds) sealed between placed stones, not bulk soil.
decisive_tests.would_show: Whether any construction-linked material predates the surface terraces.

decisive_tests.test: Independent petrographic and geochemical study of the deep columnar rock and the 'fine-grained mortar' in Units 2–3.
decisive_tests.would_show: Whether the layers are in-place weathered lava and soil, or placed stone set in made mortar.

decisive_tests.test: Rock-surface luminescence dating of buried faces of columnar blocks said to be placed, compared with columns still in natural position.
decisive_tests.would_show: Whether the blocks were moved by people (light exposure reset) or never disturbed.

falsifier: Published artifacts or features securely tied to Units 2–3, dated on short-lived material from an independent, documented excavation and older than the surface terraces, would reopen the claim.

confidence_note: Phase ages and labs now read from S1's archived full text. Terrace dates rest on a press interview (S10); the authors' artifact evidence is unpublished and unassessed.
corrections: Brief: 'construction phases back to ~27,000 years ago'. S1's oldest phase is 25,000–14,000 BCE (~27,000–16,000 yr), so ~27,000 is its upper bound. The retraction's '9000 or more years' (S2) is a lower limit, not a conflicting figure.

Brief: 'Natawidjaja et al. 2023 (Archaeological Prospection) claimed'. The team claimed deep man-made layers 14,000+ years old by 2013 (Akbar's book, S10; IAAI rebuttal, S9); 2023 was the first peer-reviewed report.
notes: Proponents' evidence (S1): columnar rock set in 'fine-grained mortar' in trenches; core logs matched to GPR, ERT and seismic layers; 32 m³ of drilling water lost at 8–14 m, read as a cavity; 14C on organic soil from within the rock layers. All authors reject the retraction: they hold the dated soils come from man-made layers with many small artifacts, sent to the journal but unpublished, and ask critics for a geological alternative (S12). TTRM earlier claimed 13,000–23,000 BCE (S9). The co-editor says peer review missed the error (S3). The 2011 Turangga Seta 'ancestral guidance' claim came from a separate group (S9). The surface terraces were never in dispute.

plates.caption: The megalithic stone terraces at Gunung Padang, West Java.

open_issues: accepted_age uses press-reported charcoal dates (S10). Yondri's chapter (S13) confirms 14C on terrace charcoal, but I could not extract its figures and calibration is unreported, so the bp values are approximate.

year_claimed 2013 is the earliest dated public claim found (Akbar's book, S10; IAAI rebuttal, S9). 2012 statements are likely, but no dated source was verified, and S9 gives no year for TTRM's 13,000–23,000 BCE claim.
multiple_labs is coded 'yes' from S1 (2023); whether both labs' dates were public by 2013–2018 is undocumented.
Declined the review's basis wording 'AMS 14C on 12 samples': S1 says 4 of the 12 were dated by the conventional method at BATAN.
Split the Dec 2023 critique instead of one 'held' objection: the association point held (S2), but natural origin of Units 2–3 stays unresolved because no published geological study shows it.
The review's detik.com source for Yondri's dates returned HTTP 404, so Tempo (S10) is used. Dropped S7 (no longer cited) and the Netflix 2022 event (not re-read, not evidential).
